name: Airbyte
description: Open-source EL platform with a huge community connector catalog and a low-code connector builder. Pick it when you want Fivetran-style ingestion but need self-hosting, connector customization, or cost control at volume.

name: Amazon Kinesis
description: AWS's fully managed streaming service family (Data Streams, Firehose) with zero-ops scaling and tight IAM/Lambda integration. The pragmatic choice for AWS-native teams that want event streaming without running Kafka; shard semantics and retention limits are the constraints.

name: Amazon SQS
description: AWS's fully managed queue: effectively infinite scale, pay-per-request, zero operations, with FIFO queues when ordering matters. The default decoupling primitive on AWS — pick it whenever you need a queue and don't need broker features like routing or fan-out (pair with SNS for that).

name: Apache ActiveMQ
description: Long-running JMS-centric open-source broker, common in Java enterprise estates; the modern Artemis engine succeeds the Classic broker. Mostly chosen for JMS compatibility with existing systems rather than for new architectures.

name: Apache Beam
description: Unified batch-and-streaming programming model whose pipelines run portably on Dataflow, Flink, or Spark runners. In practice chosen almost entirely as the SDK for Google Cloud Dataflow; outside GCP most teams write directly against the engine instead.

name: Apache Flink
description: The reference open-source engine for stateful stream processing: true event-at-a-time execution, exactly-once state, event-time windowing, and SQL. The pick for serious low-latency streaming workloads — with the caveat that operating it well takes real expertise.

name: Apache Kafka
description: The industry-standard distributed event log: durable, replayable, massively scalable, with the deepest ecosystem (Connect, Streams, Flink, every SaaS integration). The default backbone for event-driven architectures — you pick something else only when Kafka's operational weight isn't justified.

name: Apache Pulsar
description: Distributed messaging platform that combines Kafka-style streaming with queue semantics, built-in multi-tenancy, geo-replication, and tiered storage via BookKeeper. Worth picking over Kafka for large multi-tenant estates or mixed queue/stream workloads; the smaller ecosystem is the trade-off.

name: Apicurio Registry
description: Red Hat-backed, Apache-licensed schema and API registry that speaks the Confluent-compatible API while also handling OpenAPI and AsyncAPI artifacts. The genuinely open-source alternative when Confluent's licensing is a blocker.

name: Arroyo
description: Lightweight Rust stream processing engine exposing SQL pipelines with exactly-once semantics, designed to be radically easier to operate than Flink. An emerging option for teams that want serious streaming SQL without a JVM cluster to babysit.

name: AWS DMS
description: AWS's managed service for database migration and ongoing CDC replication between a wide matrix of sources and targets. The path of least resistance for lift-and-shift migrations into AWS; less compelling as a long-lived streaming CDC backbone.

name: AWS Glue Schema Registry
description: AWS's serverless schema registry integrated with MSK, Kinesis, and Lambda, with IAM-based access control and no infrastructure to run. The obvious choice for schema governance on AWS-native streaming stacks; less useful outside the AWS ecosystem.

name: Azure Database Migration Service
description: A managed service for migrating databases to Azure with support for both offline and online (minimal-downtime) migrations that continuously replicate ongoing changes. It's the Azure analog to AWS Database Migration Service (DMS). Choose it for one-time or continuous replication migrations from SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and other engines into Azure data platforms.

name: Azure Event Hubs
description: Azure's managed event ingestion service with a Kafka-compatible endpoint, so existing Kafka clients work against it unchanged. The default streaming entry point on Azure, especially feeding Fabric, Synapse, or Stream Analytics.

name: Azure Service Bus
description: A fully managed enterprise message broker with queues and publish/subscribe topics, supporting transactions, dead-lettering, sessions, and ordered delivery. It's the Azure analog to Amazon SQS/SNS or Google Pub/Sub, geared toward reliable point-to-point and fan-out messaging between decoupled services. Choose it over Event Hubs when you need per-message reliability and workflow semantics rather than high-throughput event streaming.

name: Azure Stream Analytics
description: A fully managed, serverless real-time stream processing engine using a SQL-like language over inputs like Event Hubs and IoT Hub. It's Azure's analog to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics or Google Dataflow for streaming queries, windowing, and anomaly detection. Choose it for low-ops, SQL-first streaming pipelines rather than a full Flink/Spark deployment.

name: Bytewax
description: Python-native stream processing framework (Rust/Timely Dataflow underneath) where pipelines are ordinary Python programs using the whole PyData ecosystem. The pick when your streaming logic is owned by Python-first data or ML teams who won't touch the JVM.

name: Census
description: Reverse ETL pioneer that syncs modeled warehouse data into CRMs, ad platforms, and support tools, with strong dbt integration and audience-building features. Pick it to operationalize warehouse truth into business tools without engineers writing sync jobs.

name: Cloudflare Queues
description: Managed message queue for reliable, guaranteed-delivery messaging between Cloudflare Workers, comparable to Amazon SQS or Google Cloud Pub/Sub. Its differentiator is native integration with the Workers runtime including batching, delays, dead-letter queues, and zero egress fees, letting producers and consumers stay entirely on the edge platform.

name: Confluent Schema Registry
description: The de facto standard registry for Kafka: centralized Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema storage with enforced compatibility rules on every produce. The default if you run Confluent or vanilla Kafka; licensed under the Confluent Community License, so not OSI open source.

name: Debezium
description: The de facto open-source standard for log-based CDC, streaming row-level changes from Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and more, typically into Kafka. Pick it when you need reliable, low-latency change streams and are willing to operate Kafka Connect (or Debezium Server) yourself.

name: dlt
description: Pure-Python EL library that turns any API or source into a schema-evolving pipeline with a few decorators — no platform, just code. The best fit when engineers want ingestion embedded in their own codebase and orchestrator instead of a separate connector service.

name: Estuary Flow
description: Real-time data movement platform unifying CDC and batch connectors into millisecond-latency pipelines with exactly-once delivery. An emerging pick when you want Fivetran-style ease but with genuinely streaming CDC instead of scheduled syncs.

name: Fivetran
description: Fully managed EL platform with the largest catalog of maintained connectors; you pay to never think about ingestion again. The default pick when connector breadth and reliability matter more than cost or pipeline customization.

name: Google Cloud Dataflow
description: Fully managed, autoscaling runner for Apache Beam pipelines that handles both streaming and batch data processing with a single programming model. It is the GCP analog to Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics / Managed Flink and Azure Stream Analytics. Pick it when you want serverless Beam execution for real-time ETL, windowed aggregations, and event processing without managing clusters.

name: Google Cloud Pub/Sub
description: GCP's global, serverless messaging service with automatic scaling and no capacity planning at all — closer to a giant managed queue-plus-fanout than a replayable log. The obvious pick on GCP, pairing naturally with Dataflow and BigQuery ingestion.

name: Google Database Migration Service
description: Managed service for migrating databases into Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, or Spanner with minimal downtime via continuous, change-data-capture-based replication from source engines like MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle. It is the GCP analog to AWS DMS and Azure Database Migration Service. Pick it for lift-and-shift or homogeneous/heterogeneous migrations that need ongoing CDC until cutover.

name: Grouparoo
description: Open-source reverse ETL framework that was acquired by Airbyte in 2022 and subsequently shut down; the repository is archived. Listed for recognition in existing stacks only — do not adopt for new work.

name: Hevo
description: Managed no-code pipeline platform covering EL plus light in-flight transformation, positioned as a cheaper, simpler Fivetran alternative. A pragmatic pick for lean teams that want warehouse ingestion running in days without engineering investment.

name: Hightouch
description: The other leading reverse ETL platform, evolved into a full warehouse-native 'composable CDP' with audience management and identity resolution on top of syncs. Pick it when activation needs go beyond field syncing into marketing-facing segmentation.

name: Kafka Streams
description: Kafka's client-side stream processing library: your topology runs inside your own JVM service, no separate cluster, with state backed by Kafka itself. Ideal for embedding per-service stream logic in Kafka-centric microservices; a full engine is better for heavy analytical joins.

name: ksqlDB
description: Confluent's SQL layer over Kafka Streams for defining streaming transformations and materialized views with plain SQL. Convenient for simple Kafka-native pipelines, but Confluent's center of gravity has shifted to Flink, making it a questionable bet for new work; licensed under the Confluent Community License, not OSI open source.

name: Materialize
description: Streaming database built on differential dataflow that keeps SQL views incrementally up to date with millisecond freshness, speaking the Postgres wire protocol. Pick it when you want 'a warehouse that's always current' semantics without writing streaming code; source-available (BSL), primarily consumed as a managed service.

name: Meltano
description: Open-source, code-first EL framework that turned the Singer taps/targets ecosystem into a maintainable, version-controlled tool with a proper SDK. Pick it when you want ingestion pipelines that live in git and run in your own infra rather than a vendor UI.

name: mParticle
description: Enterprise CDP with strong mobile SDK heritage, identity resolution, and consent/data-governance controls aimed at large consumer brands. Picked over Segment when mobile-first data collection and enterprise privacy requirements dominate.

name: NATS JetStream
description: Persistence layer of NATS: a single lightweight Go binary delivering streams, queues, and key-value semantics with minimal operational overhead. Excellent for edge, IoT, and microservice messaging where Kafka is overkill; not built for warehouse-scale event retention.

name: Oracle GoldenGate
description: Oracle's heavyweight enterprise replication and CDC suite, unmatched for Oracle-to-anything change capture at scale. You pick it when Oracle databases are at the center of the estate and the license cost is already a rounding error.

name: Qlik Replicate
description: Enterprise CDC and replication tool (formerly Attunity) with broad mainframe, SAP, and legacy-source coverage that open-source options don't touch. The pick when you need agentless CDC out of older enterprise systems with a supported vendor behind it.

name: Quix
description: Python-first streaming platform built around the open-source Quix Streams library, with a managed environment for deploying Kafka-based pipelines. Aimed at Python teams (notably in IoT and telemetry) who want streaming apps without JVM tooling.

name: RabbitMQ
description: The most widely deployed open-source message broker: AMQP routing, per-message acknowledgement, and mature client libraries in every language. The default for task queues and service-to-service messaging; use a log-based system instead when you need replay or very high throughput.

name: Redpanda
description: Kafka-API-compatible streaming platform rewritten in C++ — single binary, no ZooKeeper/JVM, strong tail latencies. Pick it when you want the Kafka ecosystem with dramatically simpler operations; note the core is source-available (BSL), not OSI open source.

name: RisingWave
description: Apache-licensed streaming database in Rust: Postgres-compatible SQL, incrementally maintained materialized views, and S3-backed state for cheap scaling. The open-source pick for Materialize-style streaming SQL you can actually self-host.

name: RudderStack
description: Warehouse-first customer data pipeline covering event collection, routing to destinations, and reverse ETL, with an open-source core you can self-host. The Segment alternative for teams that want the warehouse — not the vendor — to own the customer data.

name: Segment
description: The category-defining CDP: one tracking API and SDK set, hundreds of downstream destinations, plus identity resolution and audiences in the Twilio-owned platform. The safe default for event collection and routing; costs climb steeply with event volume.

name: Singer
description: The original open-source spec for composable taps and targets exchanging JSON over stdout, created by Stitch. The spec itself is effectively frozen and tap quality is uneven — today you'd consume it through Meltano rather than adopt it raw.

name: Snowplow
description: Behavioral data platform you run in your own cloud, producing rich, schema-validated event data straight into your warehouse or stream — maximum ownership and granularity. Pick it when event data quality and control matter more than plug-and-play; the core moved from Apache 2.0 to a source-available license in 2024.

name: Spark Structured Streaming
description: Spark's micro-batch streaming API, sharing the DataFrame engine and cluster with batch jobs. The pragmatic choice when you already run Spark (especially on Databricks) and second-scale latency is acceptable; pick Flink when you need true per-event processing.

name: Stitch
description: Early managed EL service built on the Singer spec, now part of Qlik (via Talend) and in maintenance mode. Reasonable for simple, low-volume replication you already have running, but rarely the right choice for new builds.

name: Striim
description: Commercial platform combining log-based CDC with in-flight SQL stream processing and delivery to warehouses and Kafka. Suits enterprises that want CDC plus transformation in one supported product rather than stitching Debezium and Flink together.

name: WarpStream
description: A Kafka-compatible streaming platform that replaces local disks and inter-broker replication with object storage, eliminating cross-AZ traffic costs and stateful brokers. It trades higher latency for radically cheaper, easier-to-operate streaming, and its agents can run inside your own cloud account.

name: ZeroMQ
description: Brokerless messaging library that embeds socket patterns (pub/sub, req/rep, push/pull) directly in your process for microsecond-level latency. Pick it for high-performance point-to-point plumbing where you accept no persistence and no delivery guarantees.
